site.title: Allen Wang | Software Engineer
site.description: Portfolio of Allen Wang, software engineer at Apple, previously at Millennium.
site.og_description: Software engineer at Apple. Stanford BS in Mathematics and Computer Science.

experience.summary: Backend services for iCloud security in Java on Cassandra, Kafka and Kubernetes.
Data platforms for quantitative research in Python and C++, with a vector database and retrieval-augmented generation.

blurb.text: Price-time priority limit order book in C++17 with average O(1) cancel, IOC, FOK and market orders, differential tests, and latency percentiles.

problem.text: An exchange holds resting buy and sell orders and has to fill each new order against the best price first, and against the oldest order first at that price. Cancels and modifies arrive about as often as new orders, so they have to be cheap too.

approach.text: Two books share one interface. MapBook keeps price levels in a std::map of FIFO std::lists and indexes every resting order by id, so a cancel unlinks it directly. FlatBook pools orders in an array and indexes levels near the best price by tick offset, so resting an order after warm-up does not allocate. A differential test runs both against a naive reference book over 20 seeds of 100,000 operations, comparing events and depth after every one.

limitations.text: One instrument, one thread, integer ticks.
No networking, persistence or market data feed.
The clock tick is 41 ns, so percentiles at or near one tick are at the clock's resolution; the throughput figures give the typical cost.

blurb.text: Three open-addressing hash maps in C++20 (linear probing, Robin Hood with backward-shift deletion, and a Swiss-table group probe), fuzzed against std::unordered_map and benchmarked across load factors.

problem.text: A hash map's lookup cost depends on how it probes and how full it is. A fair comparison fixes the capacity, varies only the load factor, and checks every table against a reference first.

approach.text: LinearMap probes the next slot and erases with tombstones. RobinHoodMap swaps an inserted entry with any entry closer to its home slot and shifts the cluster back on erase. SwissMap matches 8 control bytes at a time with bit operations on one 64-bit word. All three hash keys with a splitmix64 finalizer, and a fuzzer compares each with std::unordered_map step by step over 20 seeds.

limitations.text: One machine and one compiler for the benchmarks; CI builds and tests on Linux and macOS but does not benchmark.
Latency percentiles are averages over batches of 64 lookups, so they understate single-lookup outliers.
Keys and values are fixed at uint64_t; there is no iterator type and no custom allocator.

blurb.text: Event-driven and vectorized backtesting in Python with walk-forward testing, deflated Sharpe, portfolio optimizers and Alpaca paper trading.

problem.text: A daily backtest that trades at a price it could not have known, or that ignores costs, reports an edge that does not exist. Trying many parameter settings and keeping the best one does the same.

approach.text: The event-driven engine hands each bar to a strategy that sees data only through that bar and fills the resulting order at the next bar's open, with slippage and commission. A separate vectorized engine compiles its simulation with Numba and also trades at the next bar. The walk-forward optimizer picks parameters on a training window and scores only the following test window, and the deflated Sharpe ratio discounts the best result by the number of trials.

limitations.text: Daily bars only.
The default universe in quantsim bootstrap is today's large caps, so long backtests on it carry survivorship bias.
Cash earns nothing while Sharpe subtracts a 5% risk-free rate by default, so a mostly-cash strategy shows a negative Sharpe.

blurb.text: Pairs-trading backtester with a Kalman-filter hedge ratio, an Engle-Granger cointegration check, transaction costs and a rolling-OLS baseline.

problem.text: Two related stocks drift apart and come back together. A pairs trade bets that the spread returns to its usual level, and a backtest has to show whether that bet paid after costs on data the parameters were not tuned on.

approach.text: A Kalman filter tracks the hedge ratio and intercept as a random walk and scores each bar by its one-step innovation over the model's innovation variance. Thresholds and the filter's noise are picked on the first 60% of the period. The Kalman model and a rolling-OLS baseline then share the same signal, sizing and cost code, with 1 bp commission and 1 bp slippage per fill, and are scored on the later test window.

limitations.text: Daily closes only, and fills happen at the same close that produced the signal.
Shorting is free: no borrow fees, no margin interest, no short rebate, and cash earns nothing.
The Kalman z-score assumes white measurement noise. For real pairs whose spread is autocorrelated, the model z-score is not standardized.

blurb.text: Implied volatility surface with a bracketed IV solver, SVI smile fits and static-arbitrage checks.

problem.text: Option quotes are prices, not volatilities. Seeing the smile across strikes and expiries means inverting Black-Scholes for every quote, fitting a smooth curve per expiry, and checking that the quotes do not allow arbitrage.

approach.text: The solver rejects prices outside the model-free bounds, starts from the Brenner-Subrahmanyam guess, takes Newton steps and switches to Brent's method when a step leaves the bracket. Each expiry's out-of-the-money quotes are fitted to raw SVI by bounded least squares. The checks test monotonicity in strike, butterfly convexity, put-call parity and calendar spreads. By default the chain comes from a seeded simulator.

limitations.text: Black-Scholes is for European options. SPY options are American, so early exercise can move prices and parity holds only approximately.
The default chain is simulated. The report and its numbers come from the simulator, not from market data.
yfinance quotes are delayed and sometimes stale.

blurb.text: Prices Kalshi Fed-rate markets from futures-implied probabilities and sizes orders with fee-aware fractional Kelly. Paper mode by default.

problem.text: Kalshi lists contracts on where the Fed's target rate lands after each meeting. 30-Day Fed Funds futures already price the same question, so the gap between the two is a possible trade, once the taker fee is paid.

approach.text: Each futures price gives an average rate for its month, which pins the rate after that month's meeting. Each meeting's expected move is split between the two nearest 25 bp outcomes, and a contract's fair value is the probability of every range above its strike. Sizing shrinks the model toward the ask, adds the taker fee and scales the Kelly fraction. Paper mode records fills in SQLite and never sends an order.

limitations.text: Futures-implied rates include a term premium, so the model gives risk-neutral probabilities, not forecasts.
The model puts zero probability on anything but the two 25 bp outcomes nearest the expected move, which makes it overconfident on far strikes.
No real settled contracts have been logged yet, so there are no real results.

blurb.text: Elo, Glicko-2 and Bradley-Terry compared on simulated pairwise comparisons, with four rules for choosing the next pair, scored by how fast each recovers a known ranking.

problem.text: Ranking a pool from head-to-head results takes many comparisons. The questions are which rating system recovers the true order fastest, and whether choosing the next pair carefully saves comparisons.

approach.text: A simulator draws skills for 32 players and samples outcomes from the Bradley-Terry model. Elo, Glicko-2 and a Bradley-Terry maximum-likelihood fit rate the same comparisons. The info-gain rule picks the pair whose comparison shrinks total Glicko-2 variance the most, which is known before the outcome. Accuracy is Kendall tau against the true skills every 10 comparisons, over 100 seeds.

limitations.text: Skills are fixed, so Glicko-2's volatility, which exists for drifting skills, is not tested.
Outcomes follow the same logistic model all three systems assume. There is no test of misspecified noise.
One pool size and skill spread. Gains from active selection depend on both.

blurb.text: Swift package that ranks which contacts to nudge to stay in touch and times each nudge around quiet hours and a daily cap, with a simulator that replays a seeded synthetic year.

problem.text: A stay-in-touch app has to decide whom to remind and when. Reminders compete for a small daily budget, must skip quiet hours, and must land at the same local times across daylight-saving changes.

approach.text: Each contact's ring sets how many days can pass before it is overdue; priority grows with days overdue, and birthdays outrank drift. The engine keeps one nudge per contact, sorts by priority, kind, ring and contact ID so input order never matters, and returns at most the daily cap. The planner spreads delivery times over the rest of the allowed window. Every call takes now and a Calendar instead of reading the clock.

limitations.text: The simulation models one user and one synthetic group of contacts, and its reply, snooze and contact rates are assumptions.
The legacy baseline is a re-implementation written from a description of the old behavior, not the original code.
Delivery times are minute precision, and the planner does not account for notifications the host app has already scheduled.

blurb.text: Command-line pipeline that picks one aligned, neutral, front-facing photo of you per week or month from an unsorted photo archive and renders an aging timelapse.

problem.text: A personal photo archive has group shots, re-saved copies, relatives who look alike and long gaps. Turning it into a face timelapse means choosing, for each period, one photo where the face is yours, frontal and neutral.

approach.text: Faces are detected and embedded once and cached. Each face is compared with the seed photos nearest in time; the best match must clear a floor and beat the runner-up by a margin, or the photo goes to a review page. Survivors are filtered by pose and expression, the best per period is aligned on the eyes, the alignment is smoothed in canvas space to remove landmark jitter, and the frames are encoded to H.264.

limitations.text: The neutral filter leaks smirks and mid-blink frames, which is why the review page exists.
Tight pose and expression gates plus dedup can starve a sparse archive.
The synthetic demo shows that the stages run and filter what they should. It says nothing about detection or identity accuracy on real faces.

blurb.text: Local analyzer for an Apple Health export that fixes time zones, double-counted steps, competing sleep sources and wear gaps before any statistics, tested on a synthetic export that plants each problem.

problem.text: An Apple Health export stamps every record with the UTC offset in force at export time, counts the same steps from iPhone and Watch, and scores each night from several sleep sources. Statistics on the raw records inherit all of it.

approach.text: The build step rebuilds local time hour by hour from the export's time-zone tags, removes overlap between step sources in priority order, and picks one sleep source per night. A synthetic export plants each problem with a known answer, tests compare the output with it, and a mutation check reverts each fix in turn and requires its test to fail.

limitations.text: Zone changes are placed to within about a day, at the first tagged record in the new zone.
Before the first time-zone tag the earliest tagged zone is assumed, so those hours can be off by the difference.
The synthetic export covers the known traps, not every record type Apple writes.
